title: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
summary: Why DRAM gets stranded, how CXL.mem lets a CPU load and store device memory, what each access costs, how Linux maps it as a CPU-less NUMA node, and how tiering and pooling place pages.
outcomes: Explain memory stranding and why neither more DDR channels nor RDMA solves it cleanly
Trace a load miss to a Type 3 device through CXL.mem Req and DRS messages
Compute average miss latency for a mix of local and CXL accesses from a component latency budget
Decode a host address to a device and device offset for an interleaved CXL region
Choose between tiering, pooling and static placement, and explain TPP and Pond

lessons.title: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it

blocks.md: In the NUMA course you saw that a multi-socket server has several memory nodes and that a CPU pays more to reach a remote node than its local one. This course adds a new kind of node: memory that sits on a card or in a separate box, reached over a PCIe-style cable, but still read and written with ordinary load and store instructions. The technology is **CXL** (Compute Express Link). Before the mechanism, the problem it solves.

Memory is expensive. The Pond paper from Microsoft Azure reports that DRAM can be **50% of server cost**. Yet a lot of that DRAM sits idle for a structural reason.

A cloud host rents out virtual machines (VMs), and each VM asks for a fixed vector of resources: some cores and some memory. When every core on a host is rented, any DRAM still free on that host can no longer be sold, because there is no CPU left to pair it with. Pond calls this memory **stranded**: free, paid for, and practically unusable.

blocks.title: A toy four-host cluster: where stranded memory comes from

scenes.caption: Each host is bought with the same 512 GB of local DRAM (toy numbers, 64 cores per host). Nothing is pooled yet.
VMs fill every core on every host. The memory those VMs asked for differs per host: 384, 512, 448 and 320 GB.
With all cores rented, the leftover DRAM cannot be sold: 128 + 0 + 64 + 192 = 384 GB, or 18.75% of the 2048 GB bought, is stranded.
Pooled design: buy 384 GB per host plus a 192 GB shared pool. B borrows 128 GB and C borrows 64 GB. Total 1728 GB instead of 2048 GB, 15.6% less. D still strands 64 GB.

blocks.md: The toy cluster exaggerates the effect, but the real numbers are large too. Across 100 Azure clusters over 75 days, Pond measured about **6%** of memory stranded when 75% of cores were scheduled, over **10%** at about 85%, and up to **25%** at the 95th percentile during busy periods. Stranding is worst exactly when a cluster is full, which is when you most want the memory.

Why not just put more DIMMs on each CPU? Because the DDR interface itself is hard to widen. The *Demystifying CXL Memory* study (Sun et al., 2023) points out that a DDR5 channel needs **288 pins**, and CPU packages have a fixed pin budget. DDR is a wide, parallel bus: PCIe 4.0 moves 16 Gbit/s per lane, while DDR4-3200 moves 3.2 Gbit/s per pin, a 5x difference per wire. A serial link gives more bandwidth per pin, so a CXL memory device on a PCIe 5.0 x8 link uses about 3x fewer pins than a DDR5 channel.

The other obvious idea is to borrow memory from another machine over the network, as RDMA-based far-memory systems do. That works, but it changes the programming model: data moves by DMA into local buffers, usually triggered by a page fault or an explicit call, with more latency than CXL. Pond stresses the key difference of CXL: a cache miss to CXL memory becomes a request on a CXL port whose response brings back the missing cache line, so **neither action involves page faults or DMAs**.

CXL attacks two problems at once: capacity and bandwidth that DDR pins cannot scale (memory *expansion*), and DRAM that is stuck on the wrong host (memory *pooling*). Both rely on one property: the CPU reaches the memory with plain loads and stores, so applications do not change.

Pooling does not make stranding vanish. In the toy pooled design, host D still has 64 GB of local DRAM it cannot sell. Pooling helps because the *peaks* of different hosts rarely line up, so a shared buffer can be smaller than the sum of per-host slack.

blocks.question: A host has all 64 cores rented to VMs and 100 GB of DRAM still free. Which statement is correct?
options: The 100 GB is fine: the next VM to arrive can use it
The 100 GB is stranded: no core is left to pair with it, so it cannot be rented until a VM leaves
The 100 GB will be swapped out to free space for other hosts
The 100 GB is lost only if the host is a NUMA machine
blocks.explain: VMs need cores and memory together. With zero free cores, no new VM fits on this host, so the free DRAM is paid for but unsellable. That is the definition of stranded memory that motivates pooling.

blocks.question: Why can't a CPU vendor simply add many more DDR5 channels to every socket?
options: DDR5 does not support more than two channels per socket
Each DDR5 channel is a wide parallel interface that needs many pins (Sun et al. cite 288 per channel), and the package pin budget is fixed
More channels would make memory non-coherent
Linux cannot address more than eight memory channels
blocks.explain: DDR is a wide parallel interface. Capacity and bandwidth scale with the number of channels, and each channel eats a lot of pins. A serial CXL link delivers more bandwidth per pin, which is why it is attractive for expansion.

lessons.title: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load

blocks.md:
CXL runs on the PCIe physical layer (the same slots and electrical signaling) but adds its own link and transaction layers. On top of that wire it multiplexes three protocols:

- **CXL.io**: PCIe-style discovery, configuration, interrupts and DMA. Every CXL device speaks it.
- **CXL.cache**: lets a *device* coherently cache *host* memory.
- **CXL.mem**: lets the *host CPU* coherently read and write memory that lives on the device.

CXL 1.0 appeared in March 2019 with all three, according to the CXL Consortium's CXL 3.0 white paper.

Devices are classified by which protocols they use (Linux kernel CXL docs):

- **Type 1**: CXL.io + CXL.cache, no device memory. Example: a smart NIC that caches host data.
- **Type 2**: CXL.io + CXL.cache + CXL.mem. An accelerator such as a GPU with its own memory.
- **Type 3**: CXL.io + CXL.mem. A **memory expander**: a controller plus DRAM, no compute.

Memory expansion and pooling are Type 3 territory, so the rest of this course is about CXL.mem. The device memory the host maps is called **HDM** (host-managed device memory).

blocks.title: The path of a load that misses to CXL memory

scenes.caption: A core issues an ordinary load. If the line is in any cache level, CXL is never involved: CXL memory is cached like any other memory.
On a last-level cache miss, the physical address decides the target. Addresses in the local DDR range go to the CPU's own memory controller, exactly as in a NUMA machine.
Addresses inside a CXL window hit an HDM decoder, which routes the miss to a CXL root port. The request is a CXL.mem message, not a page fault and not a DMA.
The device's controller reads its own DRAM and sends the 64-byte line back. The line is filled into the CPU caches, so the next access to it is a cache hit.

blocks.md: CXL.mem has only a handful of message classes. Pond's Figure 1 shows the two flows that matter. A cache **miss** becomes a **Req** (request) from host to device, answered by a **DRS** (data response) carrying the line. A dirty-line **write-back** becomes an **RwD** (request with data), answered by an **NDR** (no-data response) that just says it completed.

blocks.title: CXL.mem messages for a read miss and a write-back

scenes.caption: A load misses in the last-level cache and its address belongs to a CXL window.
The host port sends a Req message over the link. Intel measured the round trip through the CXL port logic at about 25 ns.
The device answers with a DRS carrying the 64-byte line, which the host fills into its caches.
Later the line is modified and evicted. The write-back is an RwD carrying the data; the device acknowledges with an NDR. No software ran at any point.

blocks.prompt: A program running on CXL memory does `x = a[i]` twice in a row. How many CXL.mem read requests do you expect?
blocks.reveal: Usually **one**. The first load misses all caches and becomes a Req/DRS round trip. The line is then cached in L1/L2/LLC like any other memory, so the second load is an ordinary cache hit. This is a real difference from RDMA or swap-based far memory, where data must be copied into a local page before the CPU can touch it.

blocks.md: Versions in brief, from the consortium's CXL 3.0 white paper: **CXL 2.0** (November 2020) added single-level switches, persistent memory support, security and **memory pooling**, where pieces of a device can be assigned to different hosts. **CXL 3.0** moved to PCIe 6.0 signaling at 64 GT/s, added **memory sharing** (one region coherently accessible by several hosts at once) and **fabrics** with port-based routing for up to 4096 nodes.

Pooling and sharing are different. In **pooling** each slice of memory belongs to exactly one host at a time; it just moves between hosts. In **sharing** (CXL 3.0) several hosts map the same bytes at once and hardware keeps them coherent. Most CXL disaggregation designs, including Pond, use pooling.

blocks.question: A vendor ships a card with a CXL controller and 256 GB of DRAM and no compute engine. Which protocols must it implement?
options: CXL.cache only
CXL.io and CXL.cache
CXL.io and CXL.mem
CXL.mem only, because CXL.io is optional
blocks.explain: This is a Type 3 memory expander. It needs CXL.io for discovery and configuration (every device does) and CXL.mem so the host can load and store its memory. It has no cache of host memory, so CXL.cache is not needed.

blocks.question: Which statement about a CPU write to CXL memory is correct?
options: The OS takes a page fault and copies the page to the device
The store goes into the CPU cache; when the dirty line is later evicted, the host sends an RwD and the device replies with an NDR
The device DMA engine pulls the data from host memory
Writes must use special non-temporal instructions
blocks.explain: CXL.mem is plain cache-coherent memory from the core's point of view. Stores land in the cache; the eviction of a dirty line becomes a request-with-data message, acknowledged by a no-data response.

lessons.title: Worked example: what a CXL access costs

blocks.md: If CXL memory is just memory, why not put everything there? Because every miss now crosses extra hardware: the host CXL port, the link, maybe a retimer (a chip that regenerates the signal over long traces) or a switch, and the device's controller. Pond (ASPLOS 2023) gives a component-by-component latency model built from Intel's port measurements. The figure below rebuilds it.

blocks.title: Pond's latency budget for one read (ns)

scenes.caption: NUMA-local read: 40 ns in the core, caches and on-chip fabric, then 45 ns in the memory controller and DRAM. Total 85 ns.

8-socket pool (hosts wired directly to a multi-headed controller): add a host CXL port (25), wire flight time (5), the device port (25) and address check plus on-chip network (15). Total 155 ns, 70 ns more.
16-socket pool: hosts are farther away, so the link needs a retimer (5 + 20 + 5 ns). Total 180 ns, 95 ns more than local, 2.12x the local latency.

blocks.md: Two lessons hide in that budget. First, the DRAM itself is not slower; the extra time is almost all **port crossings**. Each CXL port costs about 25 ns, and a read crosses two of them. Second, distance is expensive: a larger pool needs longer cables, hence retimers, and beyond 16 sockets a switch. Pond estimates more than 270 ns (about 3.2x local) for 32 to 64 socket pools with a switch, which is why it argues for small pools of 8 to 16 sockets.
A program's slowdown depends on *what fraction* of its last-level cache misses go to CXL. With local latency $L_{loc}$, CXL latency $L_{cxl}$ and a fraction $f$ of misses served by CXL:

blocks.caption: With the 8-socket numbers: f = 0.5 gives 85 + 0.5 x 70 = 120 ns. Simplified: it ignores queuing, prefetching and memory-level parallelism, which hide some latency.

blocks.title: Average miss latency vs share of misses served by CXL

scenes.caption: 8-socket pool (155 ns). Sending half the misses to CXL raises the average from 85 to 120 ns, a 41% increase in memory latency.
16-socket pool (180 ns). The same f = 0.5 now gives 132.5 ns. The slope of the line is the extra latency per CXL miss.
Switched rack-scale pool (about 270 ns). Now even f = 0.25 costs 131 ns on average. Placement policy matters more as the pool grows.

blocks.md: Bandwidth is the more pleasant side. A DDR5-4800 channel moves 4800 MT/s x 8 bytes = 38.4 GB/s. A PCIe 5.0 x8 link at 32 GT/s carries about 32 GB/s raw *in each direction at once*. Since reads return data on one direction and writes send data on the other, Pond notes that at a typical 2:1 read:write mix an x8 CXL port roughly matches one DDR5-4800 channel. So a CXL expander adds bandwidth, not only capacity.

Do not assume every CXL device behaves like Pond's model. Sun et al. measured three real devices: one had ld latency only 35% longer than a remote-socket DDR5 node, while the other two were about 2x and 3x longer. Their bandwidth efficiency also differed widely by controller. Emulating CXL with a remote NUMA socket, as early research did, can mislead in both directions.
How much does all this hurt real programs? Pond emulated a latency of 182% of local (the 8-socket case) for 158 cloud workloads with *all* memory on the emulated pool:

blocks.title: Pond: slowdown of 158 workloads with all memory at 1.82x latency

scenes.caption: 26% of workloads barely notice (under 1% slowdown); another 17% stay under 5%. Together, 43% are fine running entirely on pool memory.
But 21% slow down by more than 25% (graph processing was among the worst hit). The remaining 36% fall in between. A blanket 'put everything on CXL' policy is not acceptable.

blocks.md: The *Demystifying CXL Memory* study found the same split from the application side: microsecond-scale services such as a key-value store saw **10 to 82%** higher tail latency with pages on CXL memory, while millisecond-scale microservice applications saw only a marginal increase, because memory latency is a small part of their end-to-end time.

Treat CXL memory as a far NUMA node: same instructions, same caching, about 70 to 100 ns more per miss for a nearby device, bandwidth comparable to a DDR channel per x8 link. Whether it is a win depends on how many misses you send there.

blocks.question: Using Pond's model (local 85 ns, 8-socket pool 155 ns), what is the average miss latency if 25% of misses go to the pool?
options: 120 ns
155 ns
blocks.explain: 85 + 0.25 x (155 - 85) = 85 + 17.5 = 102.5 ns. 120 ns would be f = 0.5; 155 ns is all misses on CXL.

blocks.question: Pond's 16-socket pool adds 25 ns more than the 8-socket pool. Where does that time come from in the model?
options: Slower DRAM chips in the pool
A retimer to keep the signal clean over a longer distance
A CXL switch with arbitration
Software page-table walks on the remote host
blocks.explain: The DRAM and controller budget is identical (45 ns). The 16-socket layout needs longer links, so a retimer (5 + 20 + 5 ns) replaces the 5 ns flight time: 30 - 5 = 25 ns more. A switch is only needed for the larger 32 to 64 socket pools.

lessons.title: From device to NUMA node: decoders, interleaving and regions

blocks.md: How does a physical address end up at the right device? CXL uses a hierarchy of **HDM decoders**. Each decoder says: this range of host physical addresses (**HPA**, also called system physical address) belongs to me, split across these targets in this pattern. At the bottom, an endpoint decoder in the device translates the HPA into a **DPA** (device physical address), an offset into the device's own DRAM.

The levels, following the Linux driver's theory of operation:

1. **Root decoders** are fixed by platform firmware. ACPI publishes them in the CEDT table as **CFMWS** entries (CXL Fixed Memory Window Structures): a base address, a size, an interleave pattern across host bridges, and restriction bits such as Type 3 and volatile.
2. **Switch and host-bridge decoders** split the range further among their downstream ports; each switch is another place where an interleave can be split.
3. **Endpoint decoders** in each memory device map their share of the range to DPA.

A configured set of decoders that maps capacity into the address space is a **region**.

**Interleaving** spreads consecutive chunks of addresses round-robin across devices so that a sequential scan uses all their bandwidth at once. Two parameters define it: the number of **ways** (devices) and the **granularity** (bytes per chunk). The Linux driver accepts power-of-two granularities from 256 bytes to 16 KB, and 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 ways, plus 3, 6 and 12 ways. Here is the 2-way, 1024-byte layout from the `cxl create-region` documentation example.

scenes.caption: The region is a contiguous range of host addresses, cut into 1 KB chunks. Which device holds each chunk is not yet decided.
Chunk number modulo 2 picks the device: even chunks go to mem0, odd chunks to mem1. A sequential read alternates devices every 1 KB.
Inside each device the chunks are packed densely: mem0 stores host chunks 0, 2, 4, 6 at device offsets 0K, 1K, 2K, 3K. No device memory is wasted on the other device's chunks.
Byte 5000 of the region sits in chunk 4 (4096 to 5119), so it lives on mem0 at device offset 2048 + 904 = 2952. The trace below computes this step by step.

blocks.title: Decoding one host address (flat modulo interleave)
blocks.code:
def decode(hpa, base, ways, gran):
    off = hpa - base            # offset inside the window
    chunk = off // gran         # which interleave chunk
    pos = chunk % ways          # which device gets it
    row = chunk // ways         # full rounds before it
    dpa = row * gran + off % gran
    return pos, dpa

pos, dpa = decode(0x1000001388, 0x1000000000, 2, 1024)

scenes.caption: Decode HPA 0x1000001388 in a window based at 0x1000000000, 2 ways, 1024-byte granularity.
The offset into the window is 0x1388 = 5000 bytes.
5000 // 1024 = 4: the address is in chunk 4.
4 % 2 = 0: interleave position 0, the first device.
4 // 2 = 2 full rounds of chunks happened before this one, so this device already holds 2 chunks.
DPA = 2 x 1024 + 5000 % 1024 = 2048 + 904 = 2952. Simplified: real hardware does this per decoder level, and some platforms use XOR instead of modulo.

blocks.prompt: You build a 4-way region with 256-byte granularity. A program streams through the first 2 KB of it. How many bytes does each device serve, and how many chunks does each device hold?
blocks.reveal: 2048 / 256 = 8 chunks, dealt round-robin to 4 devices, so each device gets 2 chunks = **512 bytes**. Device 0 holds host offsets 0 and 1024 at its DPA 0 and 256. Small granularity spreads even short bursts across all devices; large granularity keeps each page on fewer devices.

blocks.md:
Once a region exists, Linux has to hand it to software. The region driver creates a DAX device (`/dev/daxN.Y`). From there you choose:

- **devdax mode**: applications `mmap()` the device and manage the memory themselves.
- **system-ram mode**: the `dax_kmem` driver hot-plugs the range as memory blocks into the page allocator.

In system-ram mode the memory shows up as its own NUMA node with **no CPUs**, usually not local to any core. That is the far NUMA node that the prerequisite course prepared you for.

blocks.code:
# assemble a 2-way volatile region from two memory devices
cxl create-region -m -t ram -d decoder0.1 -w 2 -g 1024 mem0 mem1

# turn the resulting dax device into ordinary system RAM
daxctl reconfigure-device --mode=system-ram dax0.0

# the capacity now appears as a CPU-less NUMA node
numactl --hardware
blocks.caption: Commands from the ndctl project's cxl and daxctl tools. Device and decoder names depend on the platform.

blocks.md: Pick the memory zone deliberately. Hot-plugged CXL memory can be onlined as `ZONE_MOVABLE` or `ZONE_NORMAL`. Kernel allocations are generally not migratable and can only use `ZONE_NORMAL` or lower, so CXL memory in `ZONE_MOVABLE` serves only user pages and other movable data. `daxctl` onlines as movable by default; that keeps kernel data off the device but means CXL capacity cannot absorb kernel memory pressure.

blocks.question: A region is 2-way interleaved with 1024-byte granularity. Which device and DPA offset hold host offset 3500?
options: Device 1, DPA 1452
Device 1, DPA 428
Device 0, DPA 1452
Device 0, DPA 3500

blocks.question: After `daxctl reconfigure-device --mode=system-ram`, a process with no memory policy calls malloc and touches a new page while local DRAM has plenty of free memory. Where does the page land?
options: On the CXL node, because it is the newest memory
Interleaved across DRAM and CXL by default
On the local DRAM node; the CXL node is used only when local memory is under pressure or a policy asks for it
The allocation fails until the CXL node is bound with numactl
blocks.explain: With no explicit policy the kernel allocates from the local node first and falls back to other nodes only under pressure. The CPU-less CXL node is never local to the running CPU, so it is a fallback target unless you use numactl, mbind or tiering.

lessons.title: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond

blocks.md: Lesson 3 showed that the payoff of CXL depends on which pages live there. Two families of policy exist. **Tiering** runs inside one machine: keep hot pages in local DRAM and cold pages on CXL, moving them as their temperature changes. **Pooling** runs across a cluster: decide how much pool memory each host or VM gets, and take it back later. Linux implements the first; Pond is a published design for the second.

Linux first has to know which nodes are slow. It groups NUMA nodes into **memory tiers** by an **abstract distance**. The kernel's `mm/memory-tiers.c` computes it from firmware performance data (ACPI HMAT or the device's CDAT), relative to the default DRAM node:

blocks.caption: 576 is MEMTIER_ADISTANCE_DRAM (4 x 128 + 64), so DRAM lands in memory_tier4. Higher latency and lower bandwidth both push a node to a higher (slower) tier number.

blocks.md: Worked example with illustrative inputs: DRAM at 85 ns read and write latency and 100 GB/s each way; a CXL node at 155 ns and 50 GB/s each way. Then adist = 576 x 310 / 170 = 1050 (integer division), then x 200 / 100 = **2100**, so the CXL node is in tier 2100 / 128 = **16**, shown in sysfs as `/sys/devices/virtual/memory_tiering/memory_tier16`. DRAM stays in `memory_tier4`. Pages demoted from tier 4 go to the next slower tier.

Two kernel switches turn on tiering:

- `/sys/kernel/mm/numa/demotion_enabled`: when a fast node is under memory pressure, reclaim **migrates** cold pages to a slower node instead of swapping them to disk or zswap.
- `kernel.numa_balancing = 2` (`NUMA_BALANCING_MEMORY_TIERING`): the kernel periodically unmaps pages and catches the resulting **NUMA hinting faults**; hot pages found on a slow node are **promoted** to fast memory. `numa_balancing_promote_rate_limit_MBps` caps how fast that happens.

Meta's **TPP** (Transparent Page Placement) shaped this design. Its two key ideas: demote *proactively* so that local DRAM keeps headroom for new, short-lived, hot allocations; and do not promote a page on its first fault, only when the kernel's LRU lists say it is actually active. (Linux keeps pages on two LRU lists per node: *active* for pages recently used more than once, and *inactive* for candidates to reclaim.) The figure walks through both.

blocks.title: Tiering in action: demotion with headroom, promotion with a filter

scenes.caption: A service fills local DRAM with pages A to F. Default allocation is local first, so the CXL node is still empty. DRAM is now at its low watermark.

Reclaim runs. With demotion enabled, the coldest pages on the inactive LRU (D, E, F) are migrated to the CXL node instead of being swapped to disk. They stay mapped: a later access is a slower load, not a page-in.
New requests allocate hot, short-lived pages I and J. They land in local DRAM because TPP demoted past the allocation watermark and left headroom.

E is touched again. NUMA balancing catches a hinting fault, but E is on the inactive LRU, so TPP only marks it accessed and moves it to the active list. No migration yet: a single touch is weak evidence.
E faults again while on the active LRU: it really is hot, so it is promoted into DRAM. The filter avoids ping-pong, where a rarely used page is promoted and immediately demoted again.

blocks.md: In Meta's production tests on early CXL 1.1 hardware, TPP ran within **1%** of a baseline with all memory local, **18%** better than the Linux of the time, and 5 to 17% better than plain NUMA balancing and AutoTiering. Most of its patches were merged into Linux v5.18.

Pond solves the cluster problem differently, because a cloud provider cannot see inside customer VMs. Its building blocks:

- A multi-headed **external memory controller** shared by 8 to 16 sockets, handing out memory in **1 GB slices**. Each slice has one owner; the controller checks ownership on every access. Tracking 1024 slices for 64 hosts takes 1024 x 6 bits = **768 bytes**.
- **zNUMA**: pool memory is shown to the guest as a zero-core NUMA node, so the guest OS naturally fills local memory first.
- **Predictions**: an ML model guesses whether a VM is latency-sensitive and how much memory it will never touch (at the median, half of a VM's memory stays untouched). That untouched share is what goes to the pool.

blocks.title: Pond's control plane for one VM

scenes.caption: A VM request arrives. The scheduler asks the ML models: is this VM latency-insensitive, and how much memory will it leave untouched? Say the answer is 25% untouched.

add.label: host H needs N GB of pool

scenes.caption: The Pool Manager assigns free 1 GB slices to the host: the controller records the owner, and the host driver onlines the range. Onlining takes microseconds per GB, so the VM start is not delayed.
The VM runs. Its guest sees pool memory as a CPU-less node and touches it only if it needs more than its local share. A QoS monitor watches hardware counters for slowdown.
If the prediction was wrong and the VM slows down too much, the mitigation moves the VM to local-only memory. When the VM exits, slices are offlined (10 to 100 ms per GB) asynchronously and returned.

blocks.md: Because offlining a slice is slow, Pond keeps a buffer of free pool memory so VM starts never wait for it. Its evaluation reports performance **within 1 to 5%** of same-NUMA-node allocation while reducing DRAM cost by **7%**, and finds that pools of 8 to 16 sockets capture most of the savings. That is a smaller number than the toy cluster in lesson 1, which is the honest picture: pooling pays, but modestly, and only with careful placement.

Failure modes to watch for:

- Sending latency-critical memory to CXL: a key-value store can see tens of percent more tail latency.
- Migration overhead: aggressive promotion and demotion can cost more than it saves; Sun et al. saw a tiering policy *raise* tail latency versus a static split.
- Isolation: the kernel CXL docs warn that in Linux 6.15 and below, demotion does not respect `cpuset.mems`, so a container may end up on CXL memory you meant to keep it off.

CXL makes memory placement a policy problem again. The hardware gives you a slower, bigger NUMA tier; the operating system (tiering) or the cluster manager (pooling) must keep hot data local and push only cold or untouched data to it.

blocks.question: With demotion enabled, a server's local DRAM node hits its low watermark. What happens to a cold anonymous page that would previously have gone to swap?
options: It is compressed into zswap on the local node
It is migrated to the CXL node and stays mapped, so a later access is a slower load rather than a page-in from disk
It is dropped and re-read from the executable file
It is moved to the CXL node but unmapped until a page fault brings it back to DRAM
blocks.explain: Demotion uses page migration in the reclaim path: the page moves to the next slower tier and the page tables are updated. The program can still load it directly, just with CXL latency.

blocks.question: TPP does not promote a slow-tier page on its first NUMA hinting fault if the page is on the inactive LRU list. What problem does this avoid?
options: Deadlock between the fault handler and reclaim
Ping-pong: an infrequently used page is promoted, then quickly demoted again, wasting migration bandwidth
Running out of tier-16 memory
Breaking cache coherence on the CXL link
blocks.explain: A single touch does not prove a page is hot. Promoting it would push something else out of DRAM, and under pressure the promoted page would soon be demoted again. Requiring the page to be on the active LRU adds hysteresis.

blocks.question: Pond allocates a VM's predicted untouched memory from the pool and exposes it as a zero-core NUMA node. Why the zero-core node rather than mixing pool and local memory in one node?
options: Because CXL memory cannot be part of a node that has CPUs
Because the guest OS then prefers its local node and touches the pool only when it needs more, so correctly predicted untouched memory costs nothing
Because hypervisors cannot map CXL memory into guest page tables
Because it makes the pool memory persistent
blocks.explain: With a uniform address space the guest would scatter allocations across pool and local memory. A CPU-less node is a fallback in Linux's default policy, so the guest fills local memory first; if the untouched-memory prediction is right, the pool slices are never touched.
